guide.title: Electric potential: review guide
guide.intro: Electric potential describes the energy side of electrostatics. Because potential is a scalar, it is often easier to add than fields, and the field can then be found from how the potential changes.
guide.equationNote: Constants used in this unit: k = 1/(4πε₀) = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²), e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Prefixes: μ = 10⁻⁶, n = 10⁻⁹. 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

sections.title: Potential of point charges and uniform fields
body: Electric potential is potential energy per unit charge, V = U/q, measured in volts (J/C). Potential differences come from the field: ΔV = −∫E·dl. In a uniform field, moving a distance d along the field lowers the potential by Ed.
A point charge has V = kq/r, taking V = 0 far away. Positive charges make positive potential and negative charges make negative potential.
points: Field lines point from higher to lower potential.
Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines.
The field is the negative rate of change of potential: E_x = −dV/dx.

sections.title: Potential of charge configurations
body: Potentials add as signed numbers (scalars): V = Σkqᵢ/rᵢ, or V = ∫k dq/r for a continuous distribution. No components are needed.
A point can have zero potential but a nonzero field (the midpoint of a dipole), or zero field but a nonzero potential (the center of a ring, or of four equal charges at the corners of a square).
points: On the axis of a ring of charge Q and radius R: V = kQ/√(z² + R²).
Throughout a conductor in equilibrium, V is constant.
For a finite distribution, choose V = 0 far away.

sections.title: Energy conservation with electric forces
body: Two point charges have potential energy U = kq₁q₂/r. Moving a charge q through a potential difference ΔV changes its potential energy by qΔV. When only electric forces do work, K + U is constant.
The work needed to bring a charge from far away to a point at potential V is qV. To assemble several charges, add kqᵢqⱼ/rᵢⱼ for every pair.
points: Released charges move to lower their potential energy: positive charges toward lower V, negative charges toward higher V.
When two charges fly apart from rest, momentum conservation decides how they share the energy; equal masses share it equally.
1 eV is the energy one elementary charge gains moving through 1 V.

example.prompt: Charges of +2.0 nC and −2.0 nC sit 0.40 m apart. Find the electric potential at the midpoint, and the work needed to bring a +1.0 nC charge there from far away.
example.solution: Each charge is 0.20 m away: V = k(2.0 × 10⁻⁹)/0.20 + k(−2.0 × 10⁻⁹)/0.20 = 90 V − 90 V = 0. The work is qV = 0, even though the field at the midpoint is not zero.

misconceptions: The field depends on how V changes, not on its value: a dipole's midpoint has V = 0 but E ≠ 0.
“Potential and potential energy are the same.”
Potential is energy per unit charge: U = qV.
Potential is a scalar; add the signed values.
Positive charges do; negative charges move toward higher potential.

questions.prompt: What is the electric potential 0.30 m from a +2.0 nC point charge, taking V = 0 far away?
choiceExplanations: 200 V divides by r²; potential goes as 1/r.
18 V leaves out the division by r.
A positive charge makes a positive potential.

questions.prompt: In a uniform electric field of 500 V/m, a point moves 0.040 m in the direction of the field. How does the potential change?
questions.explanation: ΔV = −Ed = −(500 V/m)(0.040 m) = −20 V. Potential falls along the field direction.
choiceExplanations: Moving along the field lowers the potential; moving against it raises it.
12,500 divides E by d instead of multiplying.
Potential is constant only when moving perpendicular to the field.

questions.prompt: In a region, the electric potential is V(x) = 3x² − 2x volts, with x in meters. What is the electric field at x = 1.0 m?
questions.explanation: E_x = −dV/dx = −(6x − 2). At x = 1.0 m, E_x = −4.0 V/m: magnitude 4.0 V/m, pointing in the −x direction.
choiceExplanations: The minus sign in E_x = −dV/dx matters: the field points toward decreasing potential.
1.0 is V(1.0), the potential in volts, not the field.
6.0 is the second derivative of V, not the field.

questions.prompt: Four equal +q charges sit at the corners of a square, each a distance r from the square's center. Which describes the electric potential and the electric field at the center?
questions.explanation: Potential is a scalar, so the four contributions kq/r add: V = 4kq/r. The fields are vectors; opposite corners' fields cancel in pairs, so E = 0.
choiceExplanations: Potentials don't cancel: four positive contributions add up.
This swaps the two: it is the field that cancels, not the potential.
The four field vectors point in opposite pairs and cancel.

questions.prompt: A ring of radius R carries total charge Q spread uniformly. What is the electric potential at a point on the ring's axis, a distance z from its center?
questions.explanation: Every piece dq of the ring is the same distance √(z² + R²) from the point, so V = ∫k dq/√(z² + R²) = kQ/√(z² + R²). No components are needed because potential is a scalar.
choiceExplanations: kQ/z ignores that the charge is spread around the ring, farther than z from the point.
kQ/(z² + R²) uses distance squared; potential goes as 1/distance.
kQz/(z² + R²)^(3/2) is the electric field on the axis, not the potential.

questions.prompt: Along the perpendicular bisector of an electric dipole (a +q and a −q a short distance apart), which statement is true?
choices: The potential is zero everywhere along it, but the field is not
The field is zero everywhere along it, but the potential is not
Both the potential and the field are zero along it
Neither the potential nor the field is zero along it
questions.explanation: Every point on the bisector is equally far from +q and −q, so the potentials kq/r and −kq/r cancel: V = 0. The two field vectors don't cancel; they add to a field parallel to the dipole's axis, pointing from the + side toward the − side.
choiceExplanations: This reverses the two: the potentials cancel, the fields don't.
The field components along the axis add rather than cancel.
Equal distances make the potentials cancel exactly.

questions.prompt: An electron starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 1000 V. What kinetic energy does it gain? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
choiceExplanations: 1000 J treats the electron's charge as 1 C.
1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J is the energy gained through only 1 V.
Kinetic energy gained is positive; −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ J is the change in potential energy.

questions.prompt: Two protons are released from rest 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m apart and fly apart. What kinetic energy does each have when they are very far apart? (k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
choices: 0 J, because the total energy is zero
questions.explanation: The initial potential energy is ke²/r = (9.0 × 10⁹)(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)²/(1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. It all becomes kinetic energy. Momentum conservation gives the equal-mass protons equal speeds, so each gets half: about 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ J.
choiceExplanations: 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ J is the total; it is shared equally between the two protons.
2.3 × 10⁻⁸ uses ke²/r², the form for force; potential energy goes as 1/r.
The total energy is positive: like charges start with positive potential energy, which becomes kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: How much work must be done to bring a +3.0 μC charge from very far away to a point where the electric potential is 400 V?
choiceExplanations: 1.2 × 10³ J ignores the micro prefix on 3.0 μC.
7.5 × 10⁻⁹ divides q by V instead of multiplying.
